title: What does MECE mean, and how do you build a MECE structure?
description: What MECE means in plain English, how to test your own structure, and simple ways to make buckets that are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive.
hook: MECE stands for mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive: your buckets should not overlap, and together they should cover everything that matters. You build a MECE structure by splitting a problem along one dimension at a time, ideally a split that adds up (such as revenue minus costs, or one step of a process after another), then checking in a few seconds that every idea fits in exactly one bucket and nothing important is missing.
body:
Where the term comes from

The idea is usually credited to Barbara Minto, who developed it during her time at McKinsey, alongside the pyramid principle. It is now standard across consulting because it does two jobs at once: it stops a team double-counting, and it stops them missing the answer because it sat in a bucket nobody drew.

Mutually exclusive: no overlap

Each idea should belong in only one bucket. If you split a retailer's problem into "online sales" and "young customers", where does a 22-year-old buying online go? Both. Overlapping buckets lead to double counting ("online is down $1M and young customers are down $1M" might be the same $1M) and to muddled conversations.

Collectively exhaustive: nothing big missing

Together, the buckets should cover the whole problem. If you split a factory's costs into "staff" and "rent", you have missed materials, energy, maintenance and more. You do not need every tiny detail, but nothing that could plausibly hold the answer should be left out.

The easiest ways to be MECE

  • Maths splits: profit = revenue − costs; revenue = customers × spend per customer; customers = new + existing. These are MECE by definition, because they add or multiply up.
  • Opposites: internal versus external, existing versus new, short term versus long term, fixed versus variable.
  • Steps in a process: order, pick, pack, deliver. Every activity sits in one step.
  • Segments: by region, product, channel or customer type, as long as each customer or sale fits in exactly one segment.
  • Stakeholders: customers, employees, suppliers, regulators. Useful for risks and implementation.

The simple splits article has more of these for when your mind goes blank.

The 10-second test

  1. Pick any idea. Does it fit in exactly one bucket? (Exclusive)
  2. Imagine the answer to the case. Would it land in one of your buckets? (Exhaustive)

A worked example: one dimension at a time

A retailer says sales are down 10%. Splitting into "online", "young customers" and "London" fails the first test, because one sale could sit in all three. Instead, choose one dimension and quantify it:

  • Stores fell from $8M to $6M: down $2M.
  • Online grew from $2M to $3M: up $1M.
  • Total: $10M to $9M, down $1M, which is exactly the 10%.

Because the split adds up, it accounts for the whole decline: a $2M store fall partly offset by $1M of online growth. Now go one level down, in the stores only, with another clean split: store sales = traffic × average transaction value. If traffic fell 20% and transaction value fell about 6%, then 0.80 × 0.94 ≈ 0.75, which matches the 25% drop from $8M to $6M. You now know exactly where to dig, and each level of the tree is MECE on its own.

MECE when there is no equation

Strategy questions ("Should we enter Brazil?") do not add up neatly, but you can still keep buckets distinct. For example: is the market attractive, can we win against competitors, will it make money for us, and can we execute it? Then put every idea in one place only. "Local rivals cut prices" belongs under competition; the effect on margin belongs under economics. Agreeing with yourself where each idea goes is what keeps a qualitative structure MECE (see which framework to use).

What a strong answer sounds like

Weak: "I'd look at the market, customers, competitors, online, pricing and costs."
Strong: "Profit fell, so I'll split it into revenue and costs. On revenue, I'll look at volume and price by channel; on costs, fixed and variable. That covers every way profit can fall without counting anything twice."

The weak list overlaps (pricing sits inside the market and inside customers) and has no logic connecting the items.

Common mistakes

  • Mixing dimensions at one level. Channel, age and region in the same list will overlap. Use one dimension per level.
  • An "other" bucket doing the work. It makes a list exhaustive on paper but hides the thinking. Keep it small.
  • Too many buckets. Three or four at each level is easier to say and to remember.
  • Being MECE but generic. A structure that is 90% MECE and tailored to the client beats a perfectly MECE one that could apply to any company.
  • Freezing. If you notice an overlap while presenting, say so: "These two overlap a little; I'll treat pricing only under revenue." That is exactly the self-correction interviewers want to see.

Practise

1. A candidate structures a hotel's falling profit as: "occupancy, business travellers, costs, the website". What is wrong, and how would you fix it?

Show the answer

It mixes a metric (occupancy), a segment (business travellers), a P&L line (costs) and a channel (the website), so the buckets overlap. Fix: profit = revenue − costs; revenue = rooms sold × average rate, each split by segment (business and leisure); costs split into fixed and variable.

2. Give a MECE split of the reasons customers might stop buying from an online grocer.

Show the answer

One clean option follows the customer journey: they no longer need it (moved, lifestyle changed), they cannot find what they want (range, availability), the experience disappoints (delivery slots, lateness, substitutions), or a rival offers more (price, speed). Each reason sits in one stage.

3. A company's costs are split into "staff", "materials" and "marketing". Run the exhaustive test.

Show the answer

It misses rent and property, energy, technology, logistics, depreciation and overheads such as finance and legal. A safer top-level split is cost of goods sold versus operating costs, or fixed versus variable, then break each down.

Where to practise next

Use the structure drills to practise building MECE trees under time pressure, then read how to structure your answer. To decide which bucket to explore first, see the 80/20 rule in cases.
